None of the above being based on inherent or fundamental ability, but more which I put the most time into and care about getting better at.

The flip side is engineers make good money, and there isn't much chance that I'll beat or match that anywhere else. Maybe if Bitcoin hits a million 😃 and I won't need the income...

My personal opinion is that a job should be just a job and you use it to fund your passions. I think turning your hobby into a chore is a bad thing, but that's just me. I never saw the appeal in climbing the ladder of career success and I prefer keeping things I want to do casual so I am only doing them when I want to and not because I have to.

However, if you are a person who wants to put a lot of stock in their profession, doing the training might be a good idea. It depends if that is what is going to give you the most satisfaction. Put yourself in the position of retired you many years from now and ask if you would prefer to have spent your life as an engineer doing fitness on the weekends or making your life about training and coaching. Both are valid so it comes down to preference. You strike me as the type who might prefer the latter.

In saying that, I am always wary of the "follow your dreams" advice in regards to work. In the real world, things like job sustainability and income matter. You will make better money and will probably have a more stable job in engineering so questions like whether you have expensive hobbies or want a family come-up. I may be talking out of my arse about this one, but I am under the impression making big money in coaching is tough. I hear it is a tough industry in which to be so good you make a great living. Even someone like yourself who is obviously extremely fit is not guaranteed the kind of job to fund a lavish lifestyle.

One other thing I like to remember in regards to jobs is the danger of looking through romantic glasses. People tell me I should be a mechanic because I never shut-up about cars, but the expectation and reality are two different things. Being a mechanic is not the montage you see of carefully and successfully troubleshooting some intricate, satisfying problem, it is changing oil and rotating tyres on some soulless sedan. You probably understand yourself that engineering is not building spaceships as much as it is a lot of paperwork and emails, yeah? The same applies to training in that you are going to spend a lot of time explaining CICO to underwhelmed and uncooperative hamplanets and probably not as much time helping someone in the top 5% hit the top 1%. I certainly doubt that you are going to get to spend your days focusing on your own goals either because your clients need to come first. Be wary of that.

In your favour in your specific situation, I think one thing is that you could actually do both. The demand for trainers is outside the 9-5 of an engineer. You could coach part time on the weekends or even work part time in engineering and split your weeks. Not many careers offer that because most of them are going to want you at the same times. Doing that even for a little while might actually answer your question.

Is your passion for training achieving your own goals or do you specifically want to help others? Arbitrarily doing training as a career because it seems to make sense might be the opposite of what you want. If your goals are personal fitness, I honestly think you should keep that as a hobby where you can focus on you. I think fit people who take up training as a job are people who do not have the qualifications to do much else. Furthermore, people who are in those tiny percentages of achievers are people whose fitness is their job and they have trainers themselves. At the risk of assuming too much from talking so little, your fitness sounds to me like lifestyle goals rather than career goals and the money of engineering could better and more easily fund that lifestyle.

I feel like I have talked a lot and only raised more questions. :P If nothing else, keeping thinking about it. Best of luck of course (if you believe in luck ;) )

Haha. I get you. I feel the same way. Work takes up so much of your life that it does feel like a huge waste to not enjoy it or not care about it. I used to struggle with that idea a lot more. What softened me a little was after working as an electrician. I was earning buckets of money, but working very long and hard hours away from home and it beat me. The plan was to stockpile cash and get out of the rat race as soon as possible so I could live free afterwards. It turned out I couldn't sustain that much effort in a job I was only working for the money. I managed a few years doing that. What I do now earns less, but I have a much better work/life balance. What I have now is better sleep, regular hours, weekends off, etc. (read: time to actually live) and it gives me the opportunity to still spend a decent amount of time on my hobbies while still making a salary that I cannot complain about.

To an extent, I still have the same goals. Once I pay off my house, I will cut back to part time to get an even better work/life balance. It is important to me that my life is not my work, but rather that my work funds my life. I guess the lesson I learnt is that there is no "ticket out." Everyone is stuck in a job because that is how it works for the most part. That is why my advice tends to be pick something sustainable and practical. Unless you hate, hate, hate engineering, I think it's a good bet. At least for a little while, you could set-up your life really well and that will serve you well later. If you use your money wisely while you are young, you can avoid being that drone still slaving away with no end in sight in their 50s.
